cells.tense: You're tending what's yours right now, with both hands, and it's growing.
cells.verb: keeping two living things alive at once without choosing between them
cells.place: in the place where you become what you actually are
cells.ask: Let one finished thing be seen as finished — show someone what you grew and set the tools down in front of them. What comes back is care that doesn't cost you everything, and a hold that stays open.
cells.core:
You're tending what's yours right now, with both hands, and it's growing. Two things that pull against each other, and you're not sacrificing one to save the other — you keep them both alive by paying attention, not by gripping. That's not a performance of who you are. It's who you are, showing.

So the next thing isn't more tending. It's letting the tending be seen. Something you've kept alive has reached where it was going; you could let one person see that it was you, on purpose, and then let it go as done. Not as giving up — as the natural end of a job well kept. What comes back is care that doesn't cost you everything, and a hold that stays open.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping both things alive, and it's who you are.

cells.tense: You're already tending the version of this that fails if you look away.
cells.verb: gripping what grows instead of tending it
cells.place: in the place where you become what you actually are
cells.ask: Sit down with one thing that already grew and let yourself feel full of it — take in what came true before you reach for the next thing. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you, and a hold that stays open.
cells.core:
You're already tending the version of this that fails if you look away. Somewhere ahead is a season where you weren't careful enough, and you're farming against it now — checking, adjusting, carrying both ends of everything so that neither one can slip. The care is real. But it's turned into control, and control is tiring in a way care isn't. And the thing you're trying to let shine is getting managed instead of shown.

The way back isn't less care. It's letting something land. One thing you imagined has actually arrived; you could sit with it long enough to be satisfied, instead of filing it and bracing for the next one. Satisfaction is what tells the hands they can loosen. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you, and a hold that stays open.
cells.sheetLine: You can't stop tending long enough to see it grew.

cells.tense: You've let it go to seed, and you're still standing where you decided to.
cells.verb: no longer tending what was yours to grow
cells.place: in the place where you become what you actually are
cells.ask: Say the thing you'd still want to see grow, out loud, after everything — not the plan for it, just the wanting. What comes back is growth that doesn't need forcing, and a hold that stays open.
cells.core:
You've let it go to seed, and you're still standing where you decided to. Somewhere back there the careful work didn't pay — the tending went in and the growth didn't come, or it came and got taken — and you stopped putting your hands in. It made sense then. But the plot is still yours, and the part of you that only shows when you're tending something has gone quiet with it.

I'd not ask you to start weeding. That's pushing on the empty place, and it won't move. What moves it is on the other side: the wanting. Not the plan — just saying, after all that happened, that you'd still like to see one particular thing come up. Hope is what pulls the hands back toward the ground. What comes back is growth that doesn't need forcing, and a hold that stays open.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped tending it, and you're still standing where you stopped.

cells.tense: You're already keeping two things alive, and you're calling it getting by.
cells.verb: tending what grows without saying it's you doing it
cells.place: in the place where you become what you actually are
cells.ask: Tell one person about one thing you've kept alive, and say the word on purpose: "I meant to." What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you, and a hold that stays open.
cells.core:
You're already keeping two things alive, and you're calling it getting by. The balance that other people would have to work at — this and also that, neither dropped — is happening in your hands daily, and you describe it as just what has to be done. But it isn't just happening. You're doing it, carefully, and it's one of the truest things about you. It's just running without your name on it.

The simpler form of this is older than the habit of shrugging it off. It's letting the intention show. One thing you've tended, told to one person, with the words that it was deliberate and it was yours. When it's witnessed as meant, you also get to set it down when it's done — as finished, not as abandoned. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you, and a hold that stays open.
cells.sheetLine: You're already tending it on purpose. You just haven't said so.
